The third and final goal was to understand the pedestrians’ preferences and discomfort glare perceptions towards these light types and light levels. The metric development was conducted on the Virginia Smart Roads. 5.1 Methods This human factors experiment was performed on the Virginia Smart Roads, utilizing the variable lighting system, and recruited participants from the public. 5.1.1 Experimental Design A repeated measures experimental design was utilized to analyze the effects of light type and light level on perceptions of visibility, safety and comfort, preference, and discomfort glare. Safety, comfort, and visibility perceptions were assessed via a questionnaire from a pedestrian’s point of view. The independent variables used in this study and their levels are shown in Table 34. The presentation of light type and light levels was counterbalanced across participants to reduce order-related confounding effects. The experiments were conducted only when the ambient temperature was higher than 40 °F and lower than 90 °F. The experimental session took place on clear nights (no rain, fog, or snow) after civil twilight (typically after 8:00 p.m. when ambient illuminance was < 0.03 lux). Table 34. The 2000 K and 4000 K LED represent the ends of the range of commercially available CCTs for roadways. Spectral power distributions of the light types used in the study. 5.1.2.2 Light Level Overall, six light levels were selected based on the existing standards, recommended practice, and the capability of the luminaires (see Table 34). Light levels of 0.9 and 1.2 cd/m2 represent the highest light levels from the City of Cambridge during peak traffic. Light levels, 0.3, 0.45, and 0.6 cd/m2 represent the dimmed levels from the City of Cambridge. Finally, a lower light level of 0.15 cd/m2 was also used to determine its effect on pedestrians’ perceptions of visibility, safety and comfort, preference, and discomfort glare. 5.1.2.3 Age Two different age ranges were selected (18 to 35 years and 65+ years) to account for the age- related physiological changes in the eyes.
